chapterNote: Chapter 7 is the father's most vivid warning against the seductress, framed as a story he watched unfold from his own window. He first pleads with his son to bind wisdom so tightly to himself that he loves her like a sister (vv. 1-5); then, like a narrator, he recounts what he saw at dusk — a witless young man drifting toward her corner (vv. 6-9), the woman's ambush, her bold kiss, and her practiced speech of perfumed beds and an absent husband (vv. 10-20). Step by step she draws him until he follows like an ox to the butcher, not knowing it will cost his life (vv. 21-23). The chapter closes with the father's plea to all his sons: her house is a highway to Sheol, its hallways the very chambers of death (vv. 24-27).

1.text: My son, guard my words, and store up my commandments deep within you.
1.amp: My son [ben], keep [shamar — guard, watch over, preserve] my words [emer], and store up [tsaphan — hide away, treasure as something precious] my commandments [mitsvah] within you.
1.notes: shamar (H8104) is the sentry's verb, to keep watch over; tsaphan (H6845) is to hide away as treasure — the same word used in 2:1 and 2:7. The father asks the son not merely to remember his words but to bury them like buried silver, safe where they cannot be lost.

2.text: Keep my commandments and live, and guard my teaching as the very pupil of your eye.
2.amp: Keep [shamar] my commandments [mitsvah] and live [chayah — be alive, kept alive], and my teaching [torah] as the pupil [ishon — the little 'man' in the eye, its most guarded center] of your eye [ayin].
2.notes: chayah (H2421) frames obedience as the path to life itself, not mere survival. ishon (H380) is literally the 'little man' one sees mirrored in another's pupil — the body's most instinctively shielded part; the son is to guard the torah (H8451) with that same reflexive care (cf. Deut 32:10; Ps 17:8).

3.text: Bind them upon your fingers; write them on the tablet of your heart.
3.amp: Bind [qashar — tie fast, knot on] them upon your fingers [etsba]; write [kathab] them on the tablet [luach] of your heart [leb].
3.notes: qashar (H7194) is to tie or knot, the same act as binding a token on the hand (Deut 6:8). Worn on the fingers, the commandments are always in view; written on the leb (H3820), the inner seat of will, they become character, not mere reminder (cf. Jer 31:33; 2 Cor 3:3).

4.text: Speak to wisdom as a brother speaks to a sister, and welcome understanding as one of your own blood —
4.amp: Say [amar] to wisdom [chokmah], "You are my sister [achot]," and call [qara] understanding [binah] your kinswoman [moda — intimate relative, one bound to you by blood];
4.notes: chokmah (H2451) and binah (H998) are personified as the household women the son should love — sister and close kin. The intimacy of family affection is set deliberately against the counterfeit intimacy of the strange woman in the verses to follow; the son must already be bound in love to wisdom before temptation calls.

5.text: that they may keep you from the forbidden woman, from the stranger with her smooth and flattering words.
5.amp: that they may keep [shamar] you from the strange woman [ishshah zarah — the woman outside the bounds, off-limits], from the foreigner [nokriyyah] who flatters [chalaq — makes her words smooth and slippery] with her words [emer].
5.notes: zur (H2114) and nokriy (H5237) mark her as 'strange' and 'foreign' not by nation but by being out of bounds — another man's wife or no man's. chalaq (H2505) is to make smooth: her speech is frictionless, the precise opposite of wisdom's bracing words. Loving wisdom (v.4) is what arms the son against her.

6.text: For at the window of my house I once looked out through the lattice,
6.amp: For at the window [challon] of my house [bayith] I looked down [shaqaph — gazed out and down] through my lattice [eshnab — the latticed window-screen],
6.notes: the father turns storyteller. eshnab (H822) is the carved lattice through which one could watch the street unseen. From this vantage he witnesses the whole seduction unfold — a teacher's eyewitness account, lending the warning the weight of something actually seen, not merely imagined.

7.text: and there among the naive I saw, I made out among the young men, a youth with no sense at all,
7.amp: and I beheld [raah] among the simple ones [peti — the naive, easily led], I discerned [biyn] among the sons [ben], a young man [naar — a youth, still untested] lacking [chaser] heart [leb — here the seat of judgment];
7.notes: peti (H6612) is the open, gullible one of 1:4, ready to be swayed either way. To be 'void of leb' (H3820) is to lack moral judgment, for the heart in Hebrew is the seat of thought and will, not feeling. The young man's danger is not malice but emptiness — no settled wisdom to steady him.

8.text: crossing the street near her corner, taking the road that led to her house,
8.amp: passing through [abar] the street near [etsel — right beside] her corner [pinnah], and he stepped [tsaad] the way [derek] to her house [bayith],
8.notes: the youth's ruin begins with his feet. He walks 'near her corner' — not yet sinning, but courting the place of temptation, taking the derek (H1870) toward her door. Wisdom would have held his foot back (cf. 1:15; 4:14-15); folly is already drifting toward the danger it should avoid.

9.text: in the twilight, as the day declined into evening, in the deep black of the dead of night.
9.amp: in the twilight [nesheph — dusk shading into dark], in the evening [erev] of the day [yom], in the pupil-black [ishon — here the dead blackness] and gloom [aphelah] of night [layil].
9.notes: the same word ishon (H380) that named the guarded pupil of the eye in v.2 returns here for the pitch-blackness of midnight — a grim echo. Darkness is both the literal hour and the moral cover; the deeds of folly seek the night (cf. Job 24:15; John 3:19-20). aphelah (H653) is thick, calamitous gloom.

10.text: And there a woman came out to meet him, dressed like a prostitute and with a guarded, scheming heart.
10.amp: And behold, a woman [ishshah] met him with the attire [shith — the garb, the costume] of a harlot [zanah — one who plays the prostitute], and guarded [natsar — hidden, kept under cover] of heart [leb].
10.notes: zanah (H2181) carries both literal harlotry and the Bible's frequent image of spiritual unfaithfulness. The phrase rendered 'subtle of heart' uses natsar (H5341), to guard or keep hidden: her intentions are sealed away behind the costume, the opposite of the young man's open, undefended leb in v.7.

11.text: She is loud and defiant; her feet will not stay at home.
11.amp: She is loud [hamah — roaring, turbulent, clamorous] and stubborn [sarar — defiant, rebellious]; her feet [regel] do not abide [shakan — settle, stay put] in her house [bayith].
11.notes: hamah (H1993) is the roar of a crowd or a churning sea — restless, unquiet. sarar (H5637) is the willful defiance of the rebel. Her refusal to 'abide' (shakan, H7931 — the verb of God's own settled dwelling) marks her as the inversion of the wise woman who builds and keeps her house (cf. 14:1; 31:27).

12.text: Now she is out in the street, now in the open squares, lying in wait at every corner.
12.amp: Now [paam] she is outside [chuts — in the open street], now [paam] in the broad squares, and at every corner [pinnah] she lies in wait [arab — crouches in ambush].
12.notes: arab (H693) is the hunter's word, to lie in ambush — the same predatory verb used of the bloodthirsty gang in 1:11. She does not merely wander; she hunts, stationing herself where the naive will pass. The repeated paam (H6471) captures her restless prowling from spot to spot.

13.text: So she seized him and kissed him, and with a brazen face she said to him:
13.amp: So she caught hold of [chazaq — grabbed firmly, took fast grip of] him and kissed [nashaq] him; with a hardened [azaz — made bold, strong, shameless] face [panim] she said [amar] to him:
13.notes: chazaq (H2388) is to seize with strength — there is nothing shy in her advance. The idiom 'she strengthened her face' (azaz, H5810, of panim, H6440) means she put on a brazen, shameless boldness, the very face that 21:29 says the wicked man wears. Her shamelessness is a deliberate, practiced act.

14.text: "I had fellowship offerings to bring, and today I have paid my vows,
14.amp: "Peace [shelem — fellowship, peace] offerings [zebach — sacrifice] are upon me; today [yom] I have paid [shalam — completed, discharged] my vows [neder];
14.notes: the peace offering (shelem, H8002, from the root of shalom) was the one sacrifice whose meat the worshipper ate the same day (Lev 7:15-16). She cloaks seduction in piety: fresh meat from the altar waits at home, her religious duties 'paid' (shalam, H7999), and so she frames adultery as the night's celebration of a vow fulfilled.

15.text: so I came out to meet you, to seek your face with longing — and now I have found you!
15.amp: therefore I came out [yatsa] to meet [qara — encounter] you, to earnestly seek [shachar — search for at dawn, seek diligently] your face [panim], and I have found [matsa] you.
15.notes: shachar (H7836) is to seek eagerly, even at daybreak — a verb elsewhere used for the diligent search after God Himself (cf. 8:17). On her lips it is a parody of holy longing: the same earnest seeking, aimed at the youth's ruin. She flatters him that he, of all men, is the one she sought.

16.text: I have spread my couch with colored coverings, with embroidered linens of Egypt.
16.amp: I have decked [rabad — spread, layered] my bed [eres] with coverings [marbad — spreads, quilts], with carved-work linens [chatubah], the fine linen [etun] of Egypt [Mitsrayim];
16.notes: etun (H330) is fine twisted yarn; the linens of Egypt (Mitsrayim, H4714) were prized imports, a mark of luxury. She appeals through the senses, layering her speech with costly detail. The bed she boasts of will prove, by the chapter's end, a way down to the chambers of death (v.27).

17.text: I have perfumed my bed with myrrh and aloes and cinnamon.
17.amp: I have perfumed [nuph — sprinkled, sometimes the wave-offering gesture] my bed [mishkab] with myrrh [mor], aloes [ahalim], and cinnamon [qinnamon].
17.notes: nuph (H5130) is the sprinkling motion of the priest's wave offering — another sacred image bent to seduction. The same fragrances — myrrh, aloes, cinnamon — perfume the pure marriage bed of the Song of Songs (Song 4:14); here they are counterfeited, holy spices spent on an unholy night.

18.text: Come, let us drink deep of love until morning; let us lose ourselves in caresses.
18.amp: Come [yalak — come along], let us drink our fill [ravah — be drenched, sated, saturated] of love [dod — physical love, caresses] until morning [boqer]; let us delight [alas] ourselves with love-makings [ohav].
18.notes: ravah (H7301) is to be drenched or saturated — she promises love poured out to the point of drowning. dod (H1730) names the physical affection of lovers, the word that gives the Song of Songs its 'beloved.' Every term promises overflowing pleasure; not one mentions the husband she will betray (v.19).

19.text: For my husband is not at home; he has gone away on a long journey.
19.amp: For the man [ish — husband] is not at his house [bayith]; he has gone [halak] on a long [rachoq — far, distant] journey [derek].
19.notes: she calls him only 'the man' (ish, H376), not 'my husband' — a cold distance that exposes the affair. His absence on a far derek (H1870) is her assurance of safety; yet the eye she forgets is the LORD's, before whom no chamber is hidden (cf. 5:21). Secrecy is the seductress's whole confidence, and it is an illusion.

20.text: He took a bag of silver with him and will not come home until the moon is full."
20.amp: He took [laqach] a bag of silver [keseph] in his hand [yad], and at the day [yom] of the full moon [kese] he will come [bo] home [bayith]."
20.notes: kese (H3677) is the full moon, the appointed mid-month day — weeks away. The husband carries silver (keseph, H3701) for a long trade, so business and the calendar both guarantee his absence. She has thought through every safeguard; her confidence is total, and totally misplaced.

21.text: With her great persuasion she swayed him; with the smooth flattery of her lips she drove him on.
21.amp: With her abundant [rob — great, much] persuasion [leqach — teaching, winning instruction] she made him yield [natah — bent, turned him aside]; with the smoothness [cheleq — slick flattery] of her lips [saphah] she compelled [nadach — thrust, drove away] him.
21.notes: leqach (H3948) is normally good 'instruction' (cf. 1:5); here it is her persuasive art turned to evil. natah (H5186), to bend aside, and nadach (H5080), to drive or thrust away, picture a man pushed off the straight path. Her power is in words — the smooth lips (cheleq, H2506) warned of in v.5 now do their full, deadly work.

22.text: All at once he follows her, like an ox walking to the slaughter, like a fool stepping into the chains that will correct him,
22.amp: He goes [halak] after her at once [pitom — suddenly, without thought], as an ox [shor] goes [bo] to the slaughter [tebach], or as a fool [evil] to the correction [musar — discipline, chastening] of the stocks [ekes — fetters];
22.notes: the ox (shor) ambles to the butcher unaware; the fool (evil, H191) walks into fetters that bring not training but death. The bitter irony is musar (H4148) — the very 'discipline' the father has urged (1:2; 7:1ff). Refusing wisdom's discipline, the youth meets folly's: chastening too late, when it can only kill.

23.text: till an arrow splits his liver — like a bird darting into a snare, never knowing it will cost him his life.
23.amp: till an arrow [chets] pierces [palach — splits, cleaves through] his liver [kabed]; as a bird [tsippor] hurries [mahar — rushes, hastens] to the snare [pach], and does not know [yada] that it costs his life [nephesh].
23.notes: palach (H6398) is to split or cleave; the liver (kabed) stood for the seat of life and vitality — the arrow strikes the very core. The tragedy is the not-knowing: like the bird rushing (mahar, H4116) into the trap, he sins blind to the price. His nephesh (H5315), his very life, is the stake, and he never sees it.

24.text: Now therefore, my sons, listen to me; pay close attention to the words of my mouth.
24.amp: Now therefore, O children [ben], hearken [shama — hear and obey] to me, and attend [qashab — prick up the ear, listen hard] to the words [emer] of my mouth [peh].
24.notes: the father steps back from the story to its lesson, addressing not one son now but all his 'sons.' shama (H8085) is hearing that issues in obedience; qashab (H7181) is the alert, leaning-in attention of one who refuses to miss a word. The vivid tale was told for this turn — learn from the youth's ruin, do not repeat it.

25.text: Never let your heart drift after her direction; keep your steps from wandering down her trails.
25.amp: Let not your heart [leb] turn aside [satah — swerve, deviate] to her ways [derek]; do not wander [taah — go astray, lose the way] in her paths [nethivah].
25.notes: the warning aims at the leb (H3820), for the heart turns before the feet do. satah (H7847) is to swerve from the line; taah (H8582) is the lost-sheep verb, to wander off and not find the way back. The defense is inward: guard the heart's direction, and the steps will keep the road.

26.text: For she has brought down many slain; numberless and mighty are all her victims.
26.amp: For she has cast down [naphal — felled, made to fall] many [rab] wounded [chalal — pierced, slain]; and many mighty [atsum — strong, vast in number] men have been slain [harag — killed] by her.
26.notes: naphal (H5307) is to make fall; chalal (H2491) are the battle-slain, the pierced corpses. Her victims are not weaklings but atsum (H6099) — the strong and the many. Samson, David, and Solomon himself stand behind the warning: no man is too mighty to fall here. Her bedroom has the body-count of a battlefield.

27.text: Her house is the highway to Sheol, going down to the very chambers of death.
27.amp: Her house [bayith] is the way [derek] to Sheol [sheol — the grave, the realm of the dead], going down [yarad — descending] to the chambers [cheder — inner rooms] of death [mavet].
27.notes: the chapter ends where the seduction always leads. The 'inner chamber' (cheder, H2315) she boasted of — her perfumed bedroom — is revealed as the antechamber of Sheol (H7585) itself. derek (H1870), 'the way,' has run its full course: every road she offers descends (yarad, H3381) to mavet (H4194). The whole drama was a journey to the grave (cf. 2:18; 5:5; 9:18).
